questions.question: How does Spring AOP work? Explain proxies, JDK dynamic proxies, and CGLIB.
questions.title: How Spring AOP Works (Proxy, JDK vs CGLIB)
questions.direct_answer: Spring AOP creates proxies that wrap target beans and intercept method calls to apply cross-cutting concerns like transactions or caching. It uses JDK dynamic proxies when the bean implements at least one interface, and CGLIB subclass proxies when no interface is present. The proxy is transparent to callers but means that self-invocation (calling a method via 'this') bypasses the proxy and skips advice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands why @Transactional breaks on internal calls and can explain the proxy-based mechanism behind most Spring magic.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking AOP works through bytecode weaving in all cases; not knowing the self-invocation limitation or the difference between JDK proxy (interface-based) and CGLIB (class subclassing).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish Spring AOP (proxy-based, method-level only) from AspectJ (full compile/load-time weaving, field-level join points) and explain when you would reach for AspectJ.

sections.title: Why @Transactional Breaks on Self-Invocation — The Proxy Model Explained
sections.content:
The single most common AOP debugging question in Spring interviews is: 'I annotated my method with `@Transactional` but it doesn't work when called from within the same class.' Understanding why requires knowing that **Spring AOP is proxy-based**, not bytecode-based.

When Spring detects an aspect — `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, `@Async`, or a custom `@Around` advice — it wraps the target bean in a **proxy object** during the `BeanPostProcessor` phase. Every external call to that bean goes through the proxy, which applies the aspect logic (begin transaction, check cache, run on async thread). But a call from `this.method()` inside the same class bypasses the proxy entirely — it hits the original object directly.

Spring offers two proxy implementations. **JDK dynamic proxies** work when the bean implements an interface — the proxy implements the same interface and delegates to the original. **CGLIB proxies** create a subclass of the concrete class at runtime, which is why Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB (most beans don't implement interfaces). Both intercept external calls identically; neither intercepts internal `this` calls.

This proxy model is simpler and lighter than AspectJ's full compile-time or load-time weaving — but it comes with that self-invocation limitation. Knowing this trade-off and its workarounds is what interviewers test.

sections.title: How Spring Creates Proxies: The BeanPostProcessor That Replaces Your Bean
sections.content:
Proxy creation happens during the `postProcessAfterInitialization` phase of the bean lifecycle. `AbstractAutoProxyCreator` — a `BeanPostProcessor` — scans each bean for applicable advisors (aspects). If any advisor matches (e.g., a `@Transactional` method exists), the post-processor creates a proxy and **returns it instead of the original bean**.

The proxy selection follows a clear rule. If the bean's class implements at least one interface, Spring can use a **JDK dynamic proxy** — it creates a class that implements the same interface and delegates each call through an `InvocationHandler`. If the bean doesn't implement any interface, Spring falls back to **CGLIB**, which generates a subclass at runtime using bytecode generation.

Spring Boot 2.0+ defaults to CGLIB proxies even when interfaces are available, controlled by `spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true`. The reason is practical: JDK proxies require you to inject the interface type, not the concrete class. Code that injects `MyServiceImpl` instead of `MyService` breaks with JDK proxies but works fine with CGLIB. Defaulting to CGLIB eliminates this class of startup errors.

sections.title: The Self-Invocation Trap: Why this.method() Bypasses Every Aspect
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring AOP is proxy-based, not bytecode weaving** — Spring wraps the bean in a JDK dynamic proxy or CGLIB subclass; AOP only intercepts public method calls that arrive through the proxy.
- **Self-invocation bypasses the proxy** — `this.method()` refers to the original object, not the proxy; `@Transactional`, `@Async`, and custom aspects are all bypassed on internal calls — the most common AOP debugging scenario.
- **JDK proxy requires interface; CGLIB uses class subclassing** — Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB (`spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true`) because most beans do not implement interfaces and JDK proxies fail when the concrete class is injected.
- **Proxy creation happens in `postProcessAfterInitialization`** — `AbstractAutoProxyCreator` scans each bean for applicable advisors and returns a proxy instead of the original if any match.
- **AspectJ weaving is the escape hatch for self-invocation** — compile-time or load-time AspectJ modifies bytecode directly; it intercepts any method including private ones and internal calls; use it only when proxy limitations are a real constraint.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring AOP is proxy-based — not bytecode weaving. When you annotate a method with `@Transactional` or `@Cacheable`, Spring does not modify your code; it wraps your bean in a proxy object that intercepts external method calls and applies the aspect before or after delegating to the original.

**How the proxy is created**
- During `postProcessAfterInitialization`, `AbstractAutoProxyCreator` scans each bean for applicable advisors
- If any advisor matches, it returns a proxy instead of the original bean — what gets registered in the container is the proxy
- JDK dynamic proxy: requires the bean to implement an interface; Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB even when interfaces exist
- CGLIB proxy: generates a runtime subclass of the concrete class; can proxy any public method

**The self-invocation trap**
- `this.method()` refers to the original object, not the proxy — the aspect never fires
- This is the root cause of every my `@Transactional` is not working bug where one method calls another transactional method on the same class
- Fix: move the called method to a separate bean so the call crosses the proxy boundary, or inject the bean into itself

**Spring AOP vs AspectJ**
- Spring AOP: proxy-based, public methods only, no self-invocation, zero configuration overhead
- AspectJ: bytecode weaving, any method including private ones, self-invocation works — use only when the proxy limitations are a real constraint

questions.title: Pointcut Expressions — Targeting Methods in Spring AOP
questions.question: How do you write pointcut expressions in Spring AOP?

sections.title: The Pattern Language That Decides Where Your Aspect Fires
sections.content:
Every aspect needs to know **where to fire** — which methods, in which classes, under which conditions. That's what pointcut expressions define. They're a pattern language specific to Spring AOP that selects join points (method executions) based on class names, method signatures, annotations, or argument types.

Get it wrong, and your aspect either fires on every method in the application (destroying performance), misses the methods it should target (appearing broken), or — worst case — matches methods in third-party libraries and causes baffling side effects.

Spring AOP supports several pointcut designators, but three dominate production use: **`execution()`** matches by method signature pattern, **`@annotation()`** matches by the presence of an annotation, and **`within()`** matches by declaring class. The rest — `args()`, `target()`, `this()`, `@within()`, `@args()` — are niche tools for advanced scenarios.

The most important thing to understand is that Spring AOP pointcuts only match **Spring-managed bean methods**. A pointcut expression that would match a method on a non-bean object does nothing — Spring AOP works through proxies, and non-beans don't get proxied. Beyond that, Spring AOP only intercepts **public methods** by default when using JDK dynamic proxies. CGLIB proxies can intercept protected and package-private methods, but private methods are always excluded.

A well-designed pointcut is **narrow and intentional**. `execution(* *.*(..))` matches everything — every method on every bean. This causes performance issues and unexpected behavior. Prefer annotation-based pointcuts (`@annotation(Timed)`) for explicitly opt-in behavior, or tightly scoped `execution()` patterns for convention-based behavior.

sections.title: The execution() Expression: Anatomy and Common Patterns
Annotation-Based Pointcuts and Combining Expressions
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`execution()` pattern: `modifiers? return-type declaring-type?.method-name(params)`** — `*` matches one segment; `..` matches zero-or-more sub-packages in a type or zero-or-more parameters in args.
- **`@annotation()` is the safest approach for custom aspects** — explicitly opt-in; only methods carrying the annotation are matched; cannot accidentally match unrelated code.
- **Spring AOP only matches public methods on Spring-managed beans** — non-bean objects are never proxied; protected and private methods are invisible to the proxy.
- **Too-broad `execution(* *.*(..))` proxies everything** — causes measurable performance overhead on every bean and every method call; scope tightly or use `@annotation()` for precision.
- **Named `@Pointcut` methods for reuse** — extract expressions into `@Pointcut`-annotated void methods; reference by name in advice; update one place when package structure changes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Pointcut expressions are the pattern language that tells Spring AOP which methods to intercept. Get the pattern wrong and your aspect either misses everything or fires on every method in the application.

**`execution()` — match by method signature**
- Pattern: `execution(modifiers? return-type declaring-type?.method-name(params))`
- `*` matches one path segment; `..` matches zero-or-more sub-packages in a type pattern and any number of parameters in an arg list
- Example: `execution(* com.example.service..*.*(..))` matches all methods on all classes in `service` and any sub-package

**`@annotation()` — match by annotation presence**
- `@Around("@annotation(com.example.Timed)")` — only methods explicitly annotated are intercepted
- The safest approach for custom aspects — explicitly opt-in, no accidental matches on unrelated code
- Lowercase name in the designator binds the annotation instance to a parameter: `@annotation(timed)` gives you access to `timed.value()` in the advice method

**Combining expressions**
- Use `&&`, `||`, `!` to compose: `serviceLayer() && !transactional()` — service methods that are NOT `@Transactional`
- Extract reusable patterns into named `@Pointcut` void methods — update once when the package structure changes

Spring AOP intercepts public methods on Spring-managed beans only. Non-bean objects are never proxied. Private methods are always excluded.
